title: NURS 1021 Unit 1 Case Study 8
description: 24-year-old female with transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia major and cardiac iron overload after stopping chelation: pathogenesis, thalassemia major versus trait, transfusion with heart failure, deferoxamine and deferiprone.

authorReview.note: New case written by Claude on 25 Nov 2026 (NURS 1021 Unit 1, batch 3); checked against Merck Manual Professional (Thalassemias, Apr 2026). Please review (from standard references, not the Merck page): chelation regimen (deferoxamine IV/SC, deferiprone 25 mg/kg three times a day with weekly ANC); cardiac T2* thresholds (< 10 ms severe); pre-transfusion Hb goal 95–105 g/L (TIF; Merck says about 90–100 g/L); vitamin C advice; BNP (pg/mL, as MCC prints it).

question.stem: The nurse reviews the client's history and assessment. Which findings require follow-up? Select all that apply.

options.text: Height of 152 cm
Fine crackles at both lung bases and 2+ ankle edema
Shortness of breath on one flight of stairs and needing two pillows to sleep
Stopped taking deferasirox 8 months ago
Prominent cheekbones and forehead
Grey-bronze skin and a liver edge 4 cm below the costal margin
Well-healed splenectomy scar
Irregular pulse of 112 beats/min with a “racing and skipping” heart

question.explanation:
Require follow-up: each unit of red cells adds about 200 mg of iron, which the body cannot excrete, and thalassemia also increases iron absorption from the gut. Without chelation (Option 4), iron builds up in the heart, liver and endocrine glands. Iron in heart muscle causes cardiomyopathy: dyspnea on exertion and orthopnea (Option 3), arrhythmias (Option 8), and crackles and edema from heart failure (Option 2). Heart failure is the leading cause of death in thalassemia major. Bronze skin and an enlarged liver reflect iron deposited in skin and liver (hepatic siderosis), which can progress to cirrhosis (Option 6).

Long-standing, not new: marrow expansion to compensate for ineffective erythropoiesis thickens the facial and skull bones in childhood (Option 5), and severe anemia with iron overload of the pituitary and gonads limits growth and puberty (Option 1). Her spleen was removed because enlarged spleens trap and destroy transfused cells (Option 7). These need no urgent action, although asplenia raises the client's risk of severe infection.

question.stem: The nurse answers the partner's question. For each statement, click to specify whether it describes beta-thalassemia major, beta-thalassemia trait (minor), or both.

rows.text: Two altered beta-globin genes, one inherited from each parent
Usually no symptoms and no treatment needed
Severe anemia by age 1 to 2 years, needing regular transfusions
One altered beta-globin gene; the other is normal
Marrow expansion that thickens the skull and facial bones

question.explanation:
Pathogenesis: beta-thalassemia is an inherited defect in making beta-globin chains (gene on chromosome 11). With too few beta chains, excess alpha chains have no partner; they precipitate inside red cell precursors, which die in the marrow (ineffective erythropoiesis) or are destroyed in the spleen (hemolysis). Cells that survive are small and pale with target cells; nucleated red cells appear in the blood. It is common in people of Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, South Asian and Southeast Asian ancestry.

Major: both beta genes are affected (autosomal recessive), so beta-chain production is very low. Severe anemia appears once fetal hemoglobin falls, by age 1 to 2; without transfusion, the marrow expands (thick skull and malar bones, fractures), the spleen enlarges and growth fails. HbF may be up to 90%.

Trait (minor): one gene is affected; there is mild microcytic anemia, usually without symptoms, and no treatment. HbA2 above 3.5% to 4% on electrophoresis is diagnostic; it is often mistaken for iron deficiency.

Both make small cells. If the partner has beta-thalassemia trait, each pregnancy has a 50% chance of a child with thalassemia major (the client passes one affected gene to every child) and a 50% chance of a child with trait; genetic counselling is offered.

question.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

cloze.text: The client's red cells are small because [[drop0]]. The client's body has accumulated iron mainly because [[drop1]]. The nurse's priority is [[drop2]].

options.text: too few beta-globin chains are made, so cells contain too little hemoglobin
the red cells are destroyed by antibodies
the client lacks vitamin B12 to make DNA
the client lacks iron to make heme
the client eats a diet high in red meat
every transfusion adds iron that the body cannot excrete
the spleen was removed
the kidneys cannot excrete iron
body image concerns about the bones
heart failure and arrhythmias from iron in the heart muscle
liver damage from iron deposits
infection after splenectomy

question.explanation:
Small cells: hemoglobin is built from globin chains plus heme; with too few beta chains, each cell holds less hemoglobin, so cells are microcytic and hypochromic even though iron is plentiful (ferritin 2,840 µg/L). Giving iron would be harmful.

Iron overload: about 200 mg of iron enters with every unit transfused, and humans have no way to excrete extra iron; ineffective erythropoiesis also increases absorption from the gut. Chelation is started once ferritin exceeds about 1,000 µg/L or after 1 to 2 years of transfusions, and must be taken continuously.

Priority: severe cardiac iron (T2* 7 ms), a falling ejection fraction, crackles, edema and an irregular pulse put the client at risk of fatal heart failure and arrhythmias. Liver iron, infection risk and body image matter, but the threat to the client's circulation comes first.

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 1 1700 and the Orders.
question.stem: For each nursing action, click to specify whether the action is Indicated, Non-Essential, or Contraindicated.

rows.text: Infuse each unit over 3 to 4 hours and give the furosemide between units
Give oral ferrous sulfate to help the client make more hemoglobin
Tell the client that the urine may turn orange-red during the deferoxamine infusion
Give the deferoxamine as a rapid IV bolus to remove iron faster
Request a hemoglobin electrophoresis before each transfusion
Check the absolute neutrophil count every week while the client takes deferiprone

question.explanation:
Indicated: with heart failure, red cells are given slowly with a diuretic between units to prevent fluid overload. Deferoxamine binds iron to form ferrioxamine, excreted in urine and bile, which turns urine orange-red: an expected, harmless effect. Deferiprone can cause agranulocytosis, so the neutrophil count is checked every week and fever or sore throat is reported at once.

Contraindicated: the client has iron overload; iron supplements add to the damage. Rapid IV deferoxamine causes flushing, hypotension and shock; it is given by slow continuous infusion.

Non-Essential: the diagnosis is established; electrophoresis does not change before each transfusion. A type and screen (crossmatch) is what each transfusion needs.

question.stem: Which instructions should the nurse include in the client's discharge teaching? Select all that apply.

options.text: Skip deferiprone on the nights you use the deferoxamine pump
Do not take iron supplements or multivitamins that contain iron
Have your neutrophil count checked every week
Report any change in your hearing or vision
Go to the emergency department for a fever or sore throat, even if you feel well otherwise
You can stop the chelation once your transfusions are spaced further apart
Take a vitamin C 1,000 mg tablet each day to boost your energy
Carry information that you have no spleen and keep your vaccines up to date

question.explanation:
Include: deferiprone can cause agranulocytosis, and without a spleen the client is at risk of overwhelming infection with encapsulated bacteria; fever or sore throat needs urgent assessment and a neutrophil count (Options 3 and 5). Deferoxamine can damage hearing and vision (ototoxicity, retinopathy), so these are checked yearly and changes reported (Option 4). Extra iron worsens overload (Option 2). After splenectomy, pneumococcal, meningococcal and Haemophilus vaccines and medical identification are recommended (Option 8).

Do not include: vitamin C increases iron absorption and, in iron overload, can increase iron toxicity to the heart; it is taken only if the hematologist prescribes it with deferoxamine (Option 7). Iron keeps accumulating as long as transfusions continue, so chelation is lifelong (Option 6). The two chelators are prescribed together for heavy cardiac iron; skipping one reduces iron removal (Option 1).

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Month 6 1000, the Vital Signs, and the Laboratory Results.
question.stem: For each finding, click to specify whether it shows that the client's condition has improved or not improved since admission.
question.explanation:
Improved: ferritin fell from 2,840 to 1,640 µg/L and cardiac T2* rose from 7 to 11 ms (above 10 ms, less severe), showing iron is leaving the heart; BNP has normalized and edema has resolved as heart failure improved. Pre-transfusion hemoglobin is now within the 95 to 105 g/L goal, which also suppresses the marrow expansion that drives extra iron absorption.

Not improved: a neutrophil count of 0.8 × 10⁹/L (below 1.0, severe below 0.5) with a sore throat in a client on deferiprone without a spleen needs urgent action: the nurse notifies the hematologist at once; deferiprone is usually held and the client is assessed for infection.
